coreTruths.title: Universal precautions: every patient is treated as potentially infectious because carrier status is often unknown
coreTruths.broaderContext: Cross-infection control runs on a single assumption: any patient could be a carrier. That assumption, not the visible risk profile, sets the cleaning, PPE, and decontamination standard.
coreTruths.body:
## The assumption is that any patient could be a carrier

Many people who are infectious do not know it themselves [1]. So the precautions cannot be tailored to the patient sat in the chair. Universal precautions apply to everyone, every time, which is why decontamination and PPE are routine rather than risk-stratified [1].

## Refusing to treat on personal-risk grounds is unethical and discriminatory

Declining to treat a patient because their infection status feels risky is not a defensible position. It is unethical, and it can be challenged as discrimination [2]. The way out of perceived risk is the protocol, not turning the patient away.

## Cleaning is a system, not a vibe

A written infection control policy must be displayed in every surgery so the team works to the same standard [3]. Surgeries are zoned into clean and dirty areas, and only contaminated zones get disinfected, which keeps the work efficient and consistent [4]. All surfaces get cleaned at the end of every session, even ones that look untouched [5], because visible contamination is not a reliable signal.

## Staff protection sits inside the same system

New healthcare workers are tested and where appropriate inoculated against TB and hepatitis B, with hepatitis C and HIV testing added for those doing exposure-prone procedures [6]. Universal precautions protect the team as much as the patient, which is why the rules apply both ways across the chair.

citations.quote: Many patients may be unaware they are carriers of infections and therefore universal precautions are mandatory to ensure a standard cross-infection control policy for all patients.

It is unethical to refuse dental care on the grounds that it could expose the dentist to personal risk. Clinicians can be challenged on the grounds of discrimination for declining to treat a patient, or treating a patient differently, on this basis.
All staff should have documented training in cross-infection control and every practice must have a written infection control policy displayed in every surgery to ensure uniformity of procedures.
A system of zoning ↑ efficiency as only those areas which are in the contaminated zone need to be disinfected with a suitable disinfectant.
Work surfaces should be disinfected using appropriate products between patients. All surfaces should be cleaned at the end of every session, even surfaces apparently uncontaminated.

All new healthcare workers should be tested for, and where appropriate inoculated against, TB and hepatitis B, and those whose post or training requires performance of exposure prone procedures should also be tested for hepatitis C and HIV.

coreTruths.title: Every radiograph must be justified, and dose kept as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP)
coreTruths.broaderContext: Ionising radiation carries lifetime risk with no safe threshold. So each exposure has to earn its dose by changing the clinical decision, and every technique aims to keep that dose minimal.
coreTruths.body:
## Justification is per-exposure, and recorded

A radiograph is not justified by routine. Every single one taken has to be justified, and that justification recorded in the clinical notes [1]. The IR(ME)R practitioner, usually the dentist, is the person who confirms the benefit outweighs the risk before exposure [2]. If the film will not change the plan, the dose is not justified.

## ALARP shapes the day-to-day technique choices

The whole framework sits under one rule: doses kept as low as reasonably practicable [3]. That principle drives the practical defaults. Rectangular collimation for periapicals and bitewings, digital as the preferred medium, fast film if not (ISO E or faster), routine film holders, and a quality assurance programme to cut down repeats [3]. None of those are aesthetic choices, they are dose minimisation.

## Avoiding repetition is part of the dose

Every radiograph already taken is a dose already given. So they get recorded in the notes, sent with referrals, and shared with colleagues to stop the next clinician taking the same view again [3]. Each film also gets reported on in the records so the report can be reviewed later without re-imaging [3].

## CBCT does not sit inside the standard rules

CBCT doses can be significantly higher than conventional dental radiography, including doses to the operator [4]. The standard dental regulations were not built for it, so CBCT carries its own specific guidance [4]. Use of CBCT has to clear a higher justification bar than a periapical, not a lower one because the kit is in the building.

citations.quote: Every radiograph taken must be justified (and the justification recorded in the clinical notes).
Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations (IR(ME)R) practitioner The dentist responsible for justifying an exposure and ensuring the benefits outweigh the risks.
A number of requirements are necessary in order to ensure radiation doses are kept ‘as low as reasonably practicable’:

Radiation doses from CBCT (including potential doses to those operating equipment) can be significantly higher than those for conventional radiography equipment. As the existing regulations for conventional dental radiography were not sufficient to cover use of CBCT, specific guidance has been produced by the Health Protection Agency.

coreTruths.title: Clinical decisions should be guided by current evidence, with study design dictating how much weight a finding carries
coreTruths.broaderContext: Evidence-based dentistry replaces tradition and habit with study quality as the deciding factor. Where a claim sits on the hierarchy decides how confidently it should change practice.
coreTruths.body:
## Evidence-based dentistry is the framework, not an extra step

Evidence-based dentistry means current scientific evidence — research, epidemiology, audit — guides clinical decision-making [1]. It is not a parallel academic exercise. It is the lens that sorts what a clinician should rely on from what they should question.

## The hierarchy ranks claims by how well bias is controlled

Not all evidence is equal. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses sit at the top, then RCCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional surveys, with case reports and expert opinion at the bottom [2]. The well-planned RCCT is the gold standard because it minimises bias [3]. The further down the hierarchy a claim sits, the more cautiously it should change what gets done in clinic.

## Absence of high-grade evidence is normal, not an excuse

In many areas of clinical dentistry RCCT evidence is simply not available [3]. The honest position is to keep evaluating techniques and read the literature critically rather than waiting for perfect evidence or falling back on habit [3]. Cochrane exists to collate up-to-date systematic reviews across healthcare and is one of the practical entry points [4].

## Guidelines support judgement, they do not replace it

Clinical guidelines are systematically developed statements that help clinicians and patients decide on appropriate treatment for specific conditions [5]. They are guidance, not a substitute for clinical judgement [5]. To stay useful they need to be brief, practical, evidence-based, reviewed regularly, and audited for effect [5].

citations.quote: This allows the examination and application of current scientific evidence (e.g. research, epidemiology, audit) to guide the clinical decision-making processes involved in providing dental treatment.

Systematic review and meta-analysis (strongest). Randomized controlled clinical trial (RCCT). Cohort studies. Case–control studies. Cross-sectional surveys. Case series/case reports and expert opinion (weakest).

The ‘gold standard’ for clinical studies is a well-planned RCCT as these minimize the risk of bias. But in many areas of clinical practice evidence from such trials is yet not available. In the meantime, clinicians should continue to evaluate carefully the techniques they use and the results of studies reported in the literature, although the sheer volume of scientific literature makes keeping up to date a difficult task.
Cochrane aims to collate the results of systematic reviews in all areas of healthcare and ensure that the findings are kept up to date.

Defined as ‘systematically developed statements which assist clinicians and patients in making decisions about appropriate treatment for specific conditions’. They may be developed nationally or locally, but should always be seen as guidance and are not a substitute for clinical judgement. To be effective, clinical guidelines should be brief, practical, and based on the results of sound research. They should be reviewed regularly in the light of new research and their effectiveness audited.
